blood-atlas.title: The Blood Atlas
blood-atlas.lede: What is your blood telling you?
blood-atlas.blurb: The Blood Atlas is an open-source GoInvo prototype that maps more than 6,000 blood tests to the body systems and everyday concerns they relate to. Suchi Sundarraman and I made it for people who have lab results in hand and want to understand what they could point to, and what a routine panel can’t show.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.heading: Lab results arrive with little context.

blocks.text: Standard lab testing can miss the personal factors that actually shape care, and researching a result on your own usually means too much information or too little. It’s rarely clear what’s connected, what matters now and what can wait.

A routine annual panel measures fewer than 30 markers, out of the more than 6,000 blood tests in our catalogue. Most of what blood can tell you is never looked at, and people have no easy way to see that.

sections.label: My Role
sections.heading: A GoInvo project, made with Suchi.

blocks.text: Suchi Sundarraman and I made the Atlas together as an open-source GoInvo project. I designed and built the prototype, including the data pipeline behind the catalogue and the map, database and upload views.
We worked on it from July to September 2026, through several rounds of prototypes, from a symptom-based explorer and a step-by-step wizard to the map it is today.

sections.label: The Data
sections.heading: Building the catalogue first.

blocks.text: We started from LOINC, the standard code system for lab tests, and built a pipeline that turns it into one data file. Every test is tagged by body system, by who it usually comes up for (children, pregnancy, sex-specific ranges, age-based screening) and by the everyday concerns it relates to, such as fatigue, hair loss or blood sugar.

Being honest about sources mattered as much as coverage. Only about 200 descriptions are quoted word for word from a named authority such as MedlinePlus, with a link to check. The rest are written from the LOINC name and category, and the database labels them that way.

figures.alt: The Blood Atlas database: tests with their system, what they are used for, who they come up for and a source link
figures.caption: The database, with quoted descriptions marked and linked

sections.label: The Design
sections.heading: From a list of tests to a map.

blocks.text: Early versions worked like a search: pick a concern, get a ranked list of related tests. That helped people discover tests, but it stopped there and couldn’t say what a pattern of results might mean.

The Atlas now starts from results you already have. The map shows the markers in a routine panel on the left, the concerns they can point to in the middle, and the tests that would follow them up on the right. Mark a result low or high and the map shows what it could point to, including things your panel couldn’t have measured.
You can also upload a lab report PDF, such as one exported from MyChart, and the Atlas finds which results came back low or high. The file is read on your device and never sent anywhere.

figures.alt: The Blood Atlas map: routine panel markers on the left, personal concerns in the middle, follow-up tests on the right
figures.caption: The map: your panel, the concerns it points to, and what would follow up

sections.label: Outcomes
sections.heading: An open map of blood testing.

blocks.text: The Atlas is live as an open-source prototype. It doesn’t diagnose, recommend tests or know your medical history, and it says so in the app.

The idea goes further than this build. Eventually it would weigh symptoms, history, medications and past trends, and reach past a single blood draw to continuous data like wearables, to help people understand what a result means and what’s worth asking a clinician.

sections.label: What I Learned
sections.heading: Showing what we don’t know.

blocks.text: Most of what can be measured in blood is never measured in a routine checkup, and most of our own catalogue isn’t yet backed by a quoted source. Labelling both openly made the tool easier to trust.

The next step we planned is a condition layer that connects a diagnosis like iron-deficiency anemia to its symptoms, its markers and a screen-then-confirm path, so the Atlas can explain a pattern of results instead of listing related tests.

guidelines.title: Guidelines.com
guidelines.lede: Clinical answers, cited to the source
guidelines.blurb: A redesign concept for Guideline Central, the clinical guideline library used by about a million healthcare professionals a year, as Guidelines.com. I designed how clinicians could ask a question in their own words and get an answer cited to the exact paragraph of a guideline, while still browsing the library the way they already do.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.heading: Thousands of guidelines, hard to get answers from.

blocks.text: Guideline Central calls itself the largest guideline library in the world. It holds more than 3,000 clinical guidelines from over 50 medical societies and government agencies, alongside drug information, calculators, quizzes and trials, and reaches about a million healthcare professionals a year. Orphic Health worked with GoInvo on what it could become as Guidelines.com.

The content was strong, but finding an answer took work. Guidelines, drugs, trials, PubMed articles and calculators each lived in their own section with their own keyword search, which didn’t forgive typos or synonyms. Guidelines were long documents you had to scroll through, nothing showed how strong the evidence behind a recommendation was, and the mobile experience was the website squeezed onto a phone.

sections.label: My Role
sections.heading: Product designer at GoInvo.

blocks.text: I was the product designer on the project at GoInvo, working with Eric Benoit from April to June 2026. I designed and built most of the concept screens and prototypes, and kept the research, interview notes and prototypes together in one shared hub the team could edit.

sections.label: Research
sections.heading: Starting with what was already there.

blocks.text: We began with a full inventory of the current site, page by page, then looked at competing clinical reference and AI tools. We also held three interviews with people who use Guideline Central in their work, to understand how they look things up and where it slows them down.

From there we put together a feature comparison covering 16 areas, from search and navigation to evidence quality, mobile, alerts and the design system. For each one it set the current state against a recommendation for Guidelines.com and gave it a priority, so the team could agree on what to design first.

sections.label: The Design
sections.heading: An answer you can check.

blocks.text: The landing page leads with one question: what can we help you answer today? A clinician types a question in plain language and gets an answer footnoted to the exact paragraph of the guideline it comes from. Each answer shows the guideline’s own wording, the strength of the recommendation and the quality of the evidence, so it’s easy to judge how much to rely on it and then open the source.

sections.label: Key Screens
sections.heading: Keeping browse next to search.

blocks.text: Some lookups are faster by going straight to a guideline you already know, so the design keeps browsing alongside the AI answer. The new browse page replaces four separate tabs, each with a single dropdown, with one search bar and filters you can combine, such as specialty and society at the same time.

Drug monographs got the same treatment. Long prescribing information became a page with a summary of the key facts at the top, an outline of every section down the side, search within the monograph, and a link to the original document.

figures.alt: Guidelines browse page with a single search bar and a multi-select specialty filter
figures.caption: Browse: one search bar and filters that combine

figures.alt: Drug monograph page with a key-facts summary and an outline of sections
figures.caption: Drug monograph: key facts first, every section one click away

sections.label: Mobile
sections.heading: Designed for the phone from the start.

blocks.text: One of the top recommendations was to treat mobile as its own product instead of a smaller website, so I prototyped a mobile assistant for clinicians. It opens on common tasks such as finding the latest guideline, and keeps the library of guidelines, calculators, medications and trials one tap away.

figures.alt: Mobile assistant prototype for clinicians with suggested tasks and a message box
figures.caption: Mobile assistant prototype

sections.label: What I Learned
sections.heading: Trust comes from showing the source.

blocks.text: For clinicians, an AI answer is only useful if they can check it. That principle shaped every screen: no answer appears without the guideline’s own words, how strong the recommendation is, and a link to where it came from.
Starting from a full inventory of the current site also mattered. It showed how much good content was already there, so the work focused on making that content easier to reach.

ipsos-flow.title: Ipsos Flow
ipsos-flow.blurb: For two years I led design on Ipsos Flow, a single operational platform for a global research company that had never had one. Ipsos works in 50+ countries with tens of thousands of employees, on projects from $1M to $40M. Before Flow, a project’s life from pitch to fieldwork was spread across 15 tools, spreadsheets and manual handoffs.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.heading: 15 tools, and the real record lived in Excel.

blocks.text: Ipsos grew by buying companies and expanding into new regions, so by the time we started, 15 tools were in use and every country, division and team ran things its own way. The same thing had different names in different systems, workflows changed from market to market, and the real system of record was still Excel.
Nothing carried a project from one stage to the next. There was no single place to see what was going on, and important details were re-entered, or lost, every time a project changed hands.

sections.label: My Role
sections.heading: A design team of two.

blocks.text: GoInvo’s design team on this project was two people, the project lead and me. I owned the design system, the visual and interaction direction, and consistency across pods. Concepts from the project lead and other contributors came through me to become final deliverables, which I refined, made consistent and annotated with system rules so developers could build from them.
In dev audits, the project lead wrote tickets while I fixed UI issues on the spot. I also supervised and mentored the designers who joined and left during the project, on top of my own work.

Less visibly, I was the one who remembered every decision and constraint, and kept the design consistent through two years of changing scope, reorganized pods and an object model people kept disagreeing about.

sections.label: How I Started
sections.heading: Mapping how work got done first.

blocks.text: Before designing anything, I mapped how work was done at the time, using client demos, follow-up sessions with each role, document reviews and conversations with power users of each tool.

The map showed an 8-stage, 152-step workflow full of duplicated work and broken handoffs, with legacy software so hard to use that the workarounds had become the workflow. Cutting that duplication and keeping the whole project lifecycle in one place became the main goal for the platform.

figures.alt: Interactive map of the 8-stage Ipsos workflow
figures.caption: The current workflow, 8 stages and 152 steps (interactive)

sections.label: Designing Through Ambiguity
sections.heading: The data model took two years.

blocks.text: When engineering reorganized into parallel pods, product teams that each owned one area of the platform, the design system had to change with them. I rewrote the system rules so each pod could work on its own without drifting, split the designs so I could work directly with each pod owner, and added more detailed annotations and prototypes so new teams could catch up on decisions made months earlier.

The harder problem was the data model. Every major stakeholder had a strong, well-reasoned view of how it should be structured, and they were right to push, because getting it wrong would mean political tension across a large organization, slower workflows and, in the end, lost revenue.

Agreement came slowly. The same questions came up in different meetings, and each time we answered them with more evidence, including quick prototypes people could click through to feel whether a flow was right instead of arguing about it in the abstract. Nobody decided the MVP’s data model up front; we worked it out together over two years.

sections.label: The Hard Work
sections.heading: Many stakeholders, no single owner.

blocks.text: No one had the authority to make 50+ countries, with decades of local workarounds, adopt a new tool. Decisions were spread across finance, operations, research leadership, regional markets and engineering, so designs had to work for stakeholders up to COO and CTO level, each with real constraints and each able to reopen questions we thought were settled.

People disagreed about the object model for most of the project, and the scope kept changing. Workshops set a direction but didn’t always settle decisions; in the Execution pod alone, the average design decision was redirected more than 50 times before it stuck.

One of the longest debates was how closely financial data (budgets, revenue, resource costs) should be tied to execution data such as fieldwork status, deliverables and timelines. Tying them closely made it easier for teams to see and coordinate work, but caused ownership tension between finance and operations. Keeping them apart protected each team’s autonomy but kept the fragmentation we were there to fix.
We settled on a shared operational data layer with role-based visibility, which gave teams enough transparency to coordinate while respecting who owned what.

People were reluctant to leave Excel and doubted that software could handle the edge cases that had built up in spreadsheets over the years, and we had to work around political pressure without weakening the structure.

sections.label: Key Components
sections.heading: How three key screens changed.

blocks.text: From cluttered to easy to scan.

The sidebar changed in style, hierarchy, project structure and the way it presented information. Early versions were rough, and over time the to-do tasks, recommended next steps and item-type headers became clearer as we learned what people needed to see at a glance while working through a project.

Most changes came from the shifting data model, feedback from pod owners and stakeholder input, and client demos and insider feedback drove many rounds of iteration on their own. We pushed for user research and testing from the start, but the client kept saying no.
From a bold concept to a practical panel layout.

The first concept was ambitious and visually rich, built so that data gaps and status were obvious at a glance. We made it during a blind sprint, before we could see all 15 tools, and it hinted at what a deeper reorganization at Ipsos might make possible later.

Once we understood the full scope, we needed a layout that could hold a lot of dense information and still keep the data flow readable. We landed on a panel layout with a continuous tree view that shows a whole project lifecycle on one screen.
Familiar to researchers, usable by coders.

The core of the questionnaire designer is an inline editor modeled on the word processors researchers already used, with built-in guidance for writing questions correctly and standard formats that work for coders as well as researchers.
Previews and translations happen inside the editor instead of as separate steps later. We pushed for an AI layer early on, and parts of it were added later as the client came around to it.

sections.label: Outcomes
sections.heading: A working platform, piloted in 2026.

blocks.text: Interactive prototypes were our main way to test workflow assumptions across teams, reduce the risk in architecture decisions, and surface resistance early while it was still cheap to change course. They were also how we kept the client aligned throughout the project.

Those prototypes became production-ready screens, delivered as an MVP pilot for one of Ipsos’s most complex service lines. The pilot put the whole workflow in one place, brought finance, staffing and delivery data together, and tied collaboration directly to live project data.

The MVP was built and piloted in February 2026. Development is now paused after a change in Ipsos’s leadership and an internal reorganization, which is always a risk when you design for a large company that keeps changing.

figures.alt: Flow MVP pilot — live platform screenshot, February 2026
figures.caption: The MVP pilot, February 2026

sections.label: What I Learned
sections.heading: The hardest problems weren’t on screen.

blocks.text: Designing an enterprise platform is mostly about alignment and abstraction. The hardest work on this project was agreeing on shared definitions, sorting out who owned what across a spread-out company, and balancing company-wide consistency with local autonomy.
Beyond the design system, the most valuable thing I helped build was a shared operational model that teams in dozens of countries could trust and build on.

prism.title: PRISM
prism.lede: A second opinion for health handouts
prism.blurb: PRISM is a free, open-source tool that checks patient handouts, posters and videos against 23 published frameworks, such as CDC’s Clear Communication Index and AHRQ’s PEMAT. Sonia Seto and I made it for people who design patient materials and want feedback based on evidence instead of opinion.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.heading: “This looks great” isn’t feedback.

blocks.text: People who design patient materials often hear “this looks great” at handoff, and then nothing. Published score sheets exist for judging whether a handout is clear and usable, like the CDC Clear Communication Index and AHRQ’s PEMAT, but each one is a separate checklist of 20 or more items to work through by hand.
We wanted a way to check a piece against established evidence instead of opinion, before it goes out and after.

sections.label: My Role
sections.heading: Made by two designers.

blocks.text: I made PRISM with Sonia Seto of Sonia Seto Studios. I designed the tool and built the prototype, with Claude helping write and test the code, and kept a running log of every change and the reason for it.
It went from first commit to a working studio between July and October 2026, and it’s still a work in progress.

sections.label: The Rule
sections.heading: It can grade the work, but never write it.

blocks.text: From the start we set one rule: PRISM scores a draft, but nothing it produces ever reaches a patient. The writing stays with the person who made the material, and the tool’s only job is to check it against published instruments such as the CDC Clear Communication Index, PEMAT, SAM, DISCERN and IPDAS.

That rule shaped how scoring works. Only frameworks in a fixed list can be used, every score has to quote the part of the document it’s based on, and each check links to its original source. Anything the tool can’t measure from the text is left for the person to rate, and unrated items stay out of the score instead of counting as a pass.

figures.alt: The Framework Compass page listing published frameworks with links to their sources
figures.caption: The Framework Compass: 23 frameworks, each linked to its source

sections.label: The Design
sections.heading: A proofing desk for patient handouts.

blocks.text: The studio is designed to feel like a desk where someone proofs a handout against printed score sheets. The draft sits on a sheet of paper, the checks look like score-sheet rows with item numbers in the margin, and the one bright colour is highlighter yellow, used to mark flagged words.

Using it takes four steps: set a brief (who it’s for and what it is), add a draft by typing, pasting or uploading a Word file, PDF or image, pick the frameworks, then review the scores. For a phrase like “25%”, it suggests a plainer version (“1 in 4”) and names the research behind the suggestion.
Everything stays in the browser. Nothing is uploaded, and work is still there after a refresh until you clear it.

figures.alt: The PRISM studio with a material panel, a brief, framework picker and four getting-started steps
figures.caption: The studio, ready for a draft

sections.label: Outcomes
sections.heading: Free, open source and live.

blocks.text: PRISM is live as a free, open-source prototype. It checks drafts against 23 frameworks across clarity, interaction, behaviour and outcomes, and every check links back to where it comes from.
An AI evaluator, bound by the same rules, has been built and tested on its own but isn’t connected to the studio yet.

sections.label: What I Learned
sections.heading: Where to let the model in.

blocks.text: Deciding what the AI was allowed to do mattered more than any single feature. We tried letting a model write copy, name its own criteria and write citations, and cut all three, because each made the scores harder to trust.
For patient materials, a tool earns trust by showing its evidence. Every score in PRISM points to a quote and a source, and when there isn’t enough evidence, it says so.

waipo.title: Waipo?
waipo.blurb: A 20-page graphic memoir about Alzheimer’s disease across three generations, from my grandmother’s diagnosis to the science of prevention. I made it as a graduate course project, mixing family memories with medical research to turn a private conversation into something other families could use.

sections.label: The Story
sections.heading: A family story, told out loud.

blocks.text: When my grandmother, Waipo, was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, our family didn’t talk about it openly. It was a slow, confusing loss that my mom carried mostly on her own, while I watched from a distance and moved further away with every new city.

This comic is my attempt to close that distance. It started with conversations with my mom, the kind we’d never really had before, about memory, fear, genetics and what we could do. I added what I learned from the research: Alzheimer’s isn’t inevitable, and four everyday habits can lower the risk.
I didn’t want to make a medical explainer. I wanted to make something honest that shows how messy a diagnosis is, how worry passes down a family, and the small, practical reasons to stay hopeful.
Help people understand how common Alzheimer’s is, and show a calm, open way to respond to a frightening diagnosis, because it’s not the end of the world.
The general public, and especially families going through the same thing: people dealing with a parent’s or grandparent’s diagnosis while wondering about their own risk.

sections.label: Story Outline
sections.heading: The story, page by page.

steps: Drifting boats, a picture of memory coming loose.
A close moment with Waipo, and what there was to lose.
Boarding school, exchanges, then Canada, each move taking me further away.
The diagnosis arrives, and the distance suddenly feels different.
Neurons, synapses, amyloid beta and risk factors, explained through analogies and drawings.
Graduate, home for Chinese New Year
Coming home and seeing Waipo differently. She is there, but somewhere else.
Small, tender moments from her daily routine.
She no longer remembers, and there is grief in being forgotten by someone who loves you.
Concern for the family · Dialog with mom
The risk factors become personal, and my mom and I talk openly about our worries and what we can do.
Four habits backed by research, New Year’s fireworks, a family photo, and a choice to stay hopeful.

sections.label: Production
sections.heading: Rough, line, colour.

blocks.text: Every page went through the same three stages: loose sketches, clean line art, then full colour. Splitting it up let me solve one thing at a time, first the idea, then the form, then the feeling.
Teal, warm salmon and cream felt personal without being sentimental. Keeping to three colours makes every scene, from a childhood memory to a diagram of the brain, feel like part of the same story.

sections.label: Read the Comic
sections.heading: Read the comic.

sections.label: Reflection
sections.heading: What making it taught me.

blocks.text: A comic can do things a pamphlet or infographic can’t. It can stay with uncertainty and grief and still give people useful information. Public health rarely uses the form, and this project convinced me comics are a serious way to communicate about health.

Writing about my own family showed me that the more specific a story is, the more people recognize themselves in it. The more exactly I drew the way my grandmother sat on the sofa, the more readers saw their own grandmothers.
